Content:
In this lesson, we will learn how to interpret various aspects of an exponential decay expression or function.

Content:
For example, suppose that, due to overfishing, a fish population decays exponentially. The population [MATH: y(t)] is given by
[MATH: y(t) = 5\,000 \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^t,]
where [MATH: t] is the time, in months, since the overfishing began. What can we deduce about the population of fish from this model?

Content:
The first thing to notice is that the function above is an exponential decay function of the form

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = a \cdot b^t.]

Content:
So, we can deduce the following:

Content:
- [MATH: a=5\,000] represents the initial value. So this tells us that there were [MATH: 5\,000] fish when the overfishing began.
- [MATH: b = \dfrac 1 2] is the decay factor. Since [MATH: 0 < b < 1,] this tells us that we're dealing with exponential decay, not exponential growth (for exponential growth we need [MATH: b > 1]).
- [MATH: t] is the time, in months, since the overfishing began.

items.title: Interpreting Exponential Expressions

sections.normalized_html: A house was purchased for [MATH: \[math]90\,000.] Shortly after purchasing the property, the owners discovered widening cracks in the foundation. As a result, the value of the property is reduced by one-half every year. What does the expression [MATH: \[/math]\,90\,000\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^6] mean in this context?

As a result, the value of the property is reduced by one-half every year. What does the expression [MATH: \[/math]\,90\,000\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^6] mean in this context?

  • [MATH: b = \dfrac 1 2] is the decay factor.

  • [MATH: t = 6] the time, in years, since the property was bought.

Since [MATH: t=6,] the expression [MATH: \[math]\,90\,000\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^6] gives the value of the property after [MATH: 6] years.

items.title: Interpreting a Decay Rate

sections.normalized_html:
The market value [MATH: V(t)] of a car, in dollars, [MATH: t] years since it was first purchased depreciates according to the following rule: [MATH: V(t) = 25\, 000\cdot (0.95)^t]

What does the base of the exponential expression [MATH: (0.95)] mean in this context?
sections.readable_text:
The market value [MATH: V(t)] of a car, in dollars, [MATH: t] years since it was first purchased depreciates according to the following rule:
[MATH: V(t) = 25\, 000\cdot (0.95)^t]

What does the base of the exponential expression [MATH: (0.95)] mean in this context?

sections.normalized_html:
We're asked for the decay rate, so we use the decay rate formula.

The given expression is an exponential decay expression of the form [MATH: y(t) = a \cdot (1-r)^t,] where

  • [MATH: a=25\,000] represents the initial value of the car (in dollars).

  • [MATH: 1-r = 0.95,] where [MATH: r] is the decay rate.

  • [MATH: t] is the time since the car was first purchased, in years.

Solving for the decay rate [MATH: r,] we get

[MATH: 1-r = 0.95\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = 0.05.]

Now, [MATH: 0.05] (expressed as a percent) is equal to [MATH: 5\%.] Therefore, the value of the car depreciates by [MATH: 5\%] each year.

Item 8 — Example: Interpreting a Decay Rate

Example Prompt:
The market value [MATH: V(t)] of a car, in dollars, [MATH: t] years since it was first purchased depreciates according to the following rule:
[MATH: V(t) = 25\, 000\cdot (0.95)^t]

What does the base of the exponential expression [MATH: (0.95)] mean in this context?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We're asked for the decay rate, so we use the decay rate formula.

The given expression is an exponential decay expression of the form [MATH: y(t) = a \cdot (1-r)^t,] where

- [MATH: a=25\,000] represents the initial value of the car (in dollars).
- [MATH: 1-r = 0.95,] where [MATH: r] is the decay rate.
- [MATH: t] is the time since the car was first purchased, in years.

Solving for the decay rate [MATH: r,] we get

[MATH: 1-r = 0.95\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = 0.05.]

Now, [MATH: 0.05] (expressed as a percent) is equal to [MATH: 5\%.] Therefore, the value of the car depreciates by [MATH: 5\%] each year.
